name: Red Army deep operations (1941-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: Offensive doctrine in both periods: in 1941 pre-war plans and Directive No. 3 ordered immediate counterattacks (Dubno-Brody, Smolensk) that failed; 1943-45 a continuous series of front-level offensives (Glantz, Great Patriotic War and Maturation of Soviet Operational Art, DTIC ADA194152). Same value for 1941 and 1945.
weightNotes.maneuver: Mature 1944-45 value about 0.8: tank armies exploited 150 km+ into the depth (Bagration, Vistula-Oder; Glantz ADA194152). 1941-42 value about 0.3: mechanised corps shattered, tanks used in small infantry-support brigades (House ch. 4). Set between, leaning to the mature state; the snapshot's command and training ratings carry the 1941 collapse.
weightNotes.flanking: Double envelopments became the signature of 1942-45 (Uranus at Stalingrad, Korsun, Bagration, Iasi-Kishinev). In 1941 commanders deployed evenly along the front 'as if on a textbook exercise' (House ch. 4), so the 1941 value would be about 0.3.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Objectives were enemy groupings; cities were stormed late in the war (Budapest, Konigsberg, Berlin) when they blocked the axis. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Stavka held strategic reserve armies and fed them in at the decisive moment (Moscow December 1941, Stalingrad November 1942, Steppe Front at Kursk 1943); deep echelonment was central to deep battle theory (Glantz).
weightNotes.scouting: 1941 near 0.2: surprise on 22 June and repeated encirclements. 1943-45 about 0.6: reconnaissance in force before offensives, partisans and maskirovka deception that concealed the main axis (Bagration). Middle value.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.worldwars high quartile 0.355. Sourced refusal to withdraw: Order No. 227 ('Not a step back', July 1942) and tolerance of very high losses kept formations attacking or holding until exhausted (Glantz and House, When Titans Clashed). No measured share outside the backtest campaigns.
weightNotes.combinedArms: 1944-45 tank armies of tank and mechanised corps, artillery breakthrough corps and close air armies (House ch. 4; Glantz). 1941 value about 0.25: Stavka Circular No. 1 of 15 July 1941 stripped divisions of tanks and antitank units because commanders could not coordinate them (House ch. 4).
weightNotes.initiative: Highly centralised in both periods: Stavka directives and detailed army plans; junior initiative low, improving at front and army level in 1944-45. The 1937-38 purges had removed much of the officer corps (House ch. 4).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: 1943-45 offensives paused to rebuild rail and supply between operations and culminated at about 300-500 km (Vistula, August 1944); Lend-Lease trucks carried the mobile forces (House ch. 4). 1941 value about 0.3.

summary: Soviet theory of the 1930s (Triandafillov, Tukhachevsky) called for simultaneous attack through the whole depth of the enemy defence: rifle armies and massed artillery break in, then mobile groups of tanks, motorised infantry and cavalry, supported by aviation and airborne drops, exploit deep to destroy reserves and encircle. The purges and a botched 1940-41 reorganisation meant that on 22 June 1941 the Red Army was caught mid-transition; its mechanised corps were destroyed and whole fronts encircled. It survived on mass mobilisation, scorched earth, the evacuation of industry and strategic reserves, then rebuilt from 1942: tank corps, then from January 1943 coherent tank armies, artillery breakthrough divisions, deception and deep echelonment. By 1944-45 it ran successive front offensives of 150-500 km against a thinly stretched Wehrmacht.
whyItWorked: Once rebuilt, deep operations matched the Soviet strengths (mass, artillery production, T-34s, Lend-Lease trucks) against a German army with no depth. Maskirovka hid the main blow (Bagration, June 1944, destroyed Army Group Centre), massed artillery broke the defence, and tank armies exploited before German reserves could react. Defensively, the deep belts at Kursk (July 1943) absorbed the last major German offensive in the east.
whereItFailed: 1941: Bialystok-Minsk, Kiev (the largest encirclement of the war) and Vyazma-Bryansk cost several million men, mostly prisoners, because the Red Army was untrained in its own doctrine and ordered into hopeless counterattacks. Finland 1939-40 showed it could not coordinate a deliberate attack. Kharkov, May 1942, an offensive that walked into encirclement; Operation Mars at Rzhev, November-December 1942, a costly failure; Third Kharkov, February-March 1943, after advancing beyond supply. Even successful operations cost far more men than the German defenders lost (Prokhorovka, the Seelow Heights).
